Wider sanctions relief, which will not be offered until the nuclear negotiations are completed to mutual satisfaction, would cover primary and secondary sanctions as well as UN sanctions. If this happened, it would represent the biggest recasting of US-Iran relations since the Iranian revolution in 1979.

What is worse from the US perspective is that all these concessions have been made to try to secure the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, which was open before the war, but even that may not be achieved.

The memorandum text shows that free navigation of the strait could end after 60 days, at which point Iran will conduct dialogue with Oman to define the future administration and maritime services in the strait in discussion with other Gulf states.

Finally, there is a proposed $350bn Iran reconstruction fund that the US has said it will create but will not contribute to. For that amount of money – the equivalent of the financial losses Iran has suffered – to be raised, the Gulf states would have to be deeply forgiving to a country that has just bombed their hotels and airbases and frozen their economies.

Nothing, even the unfreezing of the $24bn Iranian assets abroad, is likely to do much to ease Iran’s acute economies woes.

More importantly, the 2015 deal was a fully fledged arms control document. The memorandum is at best a document that sets the stage for another negotiation that could end up in a stalemate or an agreement closely resembling the 2015 deal.

Apart from the Iranian reiteration that it does not seek a nuclear weapon, the scope of the nuclear talks is left entirely open. The memorandum’s language is not even as strong as the 2015 agreement where Iran reaffirmed that “under no circumstances will Iran ever seek, develop or acquire nuclear weapons”.

Sometimes persistence helps you achieve things that others think are impossible. But there are also situations where being unwilling to reconsider a decision can become far more expensive than listening to expert advice.

A recent case in the United States is a good example.

As part of the preparations for the 250th anniversary of American independence, the famous Reflecting Pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial was renovated. The project was personally supported by Donald Trump, who wanted the pool to have a more striking appearance. To achieve this, the bottom was repainted in a darker shade called "American Flag Blue."

The project was originally announced with a budget of $1.5 million, but the final cost reached $14.6 million.

Before construction even began, multiple experts warned that the darker surface would absorb more sunlight, increasing the water temperature and creating almost perfect conditions for algae growth.

Despite those warnings, the decision remained unchanged.

The results appeared remarkably quickly.
On June 3, 2026, the renovation was officially declared complete. By June 14 - less than two weeks later - the water had turned green due to a massive algae bloom.
Employees of the  National Park Service had to respond after the reopening by treating the water with hydrogen peroxide in an effort to control the outbreak.

Experts later explained why this happened.
The president of Pool Service Company pointed out that pumping untreated river water into the pool already creates favorable conditions for algae.
Brooks Barrett, a marine biologist at the Smithsonian Institution, described the Reflecting Pool as almost an ideal environment for algae growth: warm water, very little circulation, and abundant sunlight.
Alla Silkina, a biologist at Swansea University, added that the darker bottom selected for the project absorbs even more solar radiation, further warming the water and accelerating algae growth.

This story is not really about politics. It is about decision-making.
Sometimes confidence in an idea becomes so strong that expert opinions are pushed aside. Yet situations like this remind us of something simple: scientific knowledge and practical experience are not obstacles to innovation - they are often what make good ideas succeed in the real world.
